title: SEVEN BASKETS LEFT OVER: THE MIRACLE JESUS PERFORMED AFTER EVERYONE HAD EATEN
paragraphs: SEVEN BASKETS LEFT OVER: THE MIRACLE JESUS PERFORMED AFTER EVERYONE HAD EATEN
Four thousand hungry people. Seven loaves of bread. One compassionate Savior. And seven baskets of leftovers that reveal something extraordinary about the heart of Jesus Christ.
What if the most overlooked part of this miracle is the very thing your exhausted soul needs to hear today?
Everyone remembers that Jesus fed the hungry.
But something happened after the miracle that most people read right past.
The crowd had eaten. The hunger was gone. The impossible had happened.
And still, there was bread left over.
Not a few crumbs scattered across the ground.
Not one small piece saved for later.
Seven baskets. Full.
Why seven?
Why did Jesus allow so much to remain?
And why did Matthew, writing under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, make sure we knew the exact number?
Because those baskets belonged to a story much bigger than bread.
And when you understand what Scripture actually reveals about this miracle, you may never read Matthew 15:37 the same way again.
Especially if you have ever looked at your life and wondered whether there could possibly be enough grace left for someone like you.
There is something you need to see.
But first, you need to understand where this miracle happened, who was standing in front of Jesus, and why the compassion of Christ makes this account so extraordinary.
Because the seven baskets were not the beginning of the story.
They were what remained after mercy had already done its work.
Matthew 15 opens with a confrontation.
Religious leaders from Jerusalem questioned Jesus because His disciples did not follow the traditional ceremonial handwashing practices of the elders.
Jesus responded by exposing something far more serious than unwashed hands.
He confronted hearts that honored God with religious language while remaining distant from Him.
Quoting Isaiah, Jesus declared:
“This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.” — Matthew 15:8, KJV
Think about that.
People could appear religious, defend their traditions, and speak respectfully about God while their hearts remained far away from Him.
And that danger has never disappeared.
You can know the worship songs.
You can post Bible verses.
You can attend church every Sunday.
You can even tell everyone that God has been good to you.
Yet somewhere beneath the carefully maintained appearance, your heart can be exhausted, distracted, proud, wounded, or quietly drifting away from Jesus.
And sometimes the most frightening spiritual condition is not open rebellion.
It is becoming comfortable with a version of Christianity that looks alive on the outside while slowly growing cold within.
Jesus was not interested in religious performance without genuine devotion.
He came to deal with the human heart.
And what happens next in Matthew 15 shows just how far His mercy reaches.
A Canaanite woman approached Jesus, pleading for her daughter, who was terribly oppressed by a demon.
She was an outsider to Israel's covenant community.
Her situation was desperate.
And the conversation that followed tested and revealed the extraordinary persistence of her faith.
She cried:
“Lord, help me.” — Matthew 15:25, KJV
Three words.
No impressive speech.
No attempt to prove herself worthy.
Just desperation reaching toward the only One who could help.
Jesus ultimately commended her:
“O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt.” — Matthew 15:28, KJV
And her daughter was healed.
Then Matthew tells us that Jesus traveled beside the Sea of Galilee, went up on a mountain, and sat down.
Great crowds came to Him.
They brought the lame, the blind, the mute, the maimed, and many others.
They laid them at His feet.
And Jesus healed them.
Imagine standing there.
Someone who had never walked suddenly standing upright.
Someone who had lived in darkness opening their eyes to the world.
Families weeping.
People staring at hands and feet that had been restored.
And through it all, the crowds glorified the God of Israel.
That detail matters.
Matthew 15:31 specifically says they glorified “the God of Israel.”
Some interpreters understand this wording, together with the surrounding geographical and narrative context, as suggesting a significant Gentile presence among the crowds.
That is a reasonable interpretation, although Matthew does not explicitly identify every person in the gathering as a Gentile.
We must be careful not to turn a strong possibility into a claim Scripture never directly makes.
But the larger movement of the chapter is unmistakable.

The mercy of Jesus is being displayed in a setting that follows His encounter with a Canaanite woman, and His compassion is reaching people whose needs are far greater than anything they can provide for themselves.
Then something happens.
Something painfully ordinary.
The people become hungry.
Not spiritually hungry in some merely symbolic sense.
Physically hungry.
Their stomachs are empty.
Their strength is running low.
And they are far from the ordinary places where food might be found.
Jesus calls His disciples and says:
“I have compassion on the multitude, because they continue with me now three days, and have nothing to eat: and I will not send them away fasting, lest they faint in the way.” — Matthew 15:32, KJV
Read those words again.
“I have compassion.”
Before the bread multiplied, compassion moved the heart of Christ.
Before anyone asked for another miracle, Jesus recognized their need.
Before the disciples discovered a solution, the Savior had already seen the problem.
The Greek word translated “I have compassion” is σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai).
It describes being deeply moved with compassion.
Not detached concern.
Not cold observation.
Not the kind of sympathy that notices suffering and then walks away.
It communicates profound, heartfelt mercy.
And Matthew uses this language to describe Jesus.
That should stop us.
The One through whom all things were made was concerned that ordinary people might collapse from hunger on their journey home.
The eternal Son of God cared about tired bodies.
Empty stomachs.
Long roads.
Human weakness.
Sometimes we imagine that God is interested only in the dramatic parts of our lives.
Our salvation.
Our calling.
Our biggest decisions.
Our most visible spiritual battles.
But here is Jesus, concerned about whether people have enough strength to make it home.
He did not regard their physical weakness as beneath His attention.
And perhaps that matters to someone reading this who has been quietly carrying more than anyone realizes.
You have been trying to remain faithful while your finances are stretched.
You have been praying while your marriage feels fragile.
You have been caring for everyone else while privately wondering how much longer you can continue.
You have been smiling in church while fighting tears in the parking lot.
You have been telling people, “I'm okay,” because explaining the truth would take more strength than you have left.
And you wonder whether Jesus sees any of it.
Matthew 15 does not promise that every difficulty will disappear immediately.
But it reveals something we desperately need to remember.
Jesus is not indifferent to human weakness.
He saw the crowd.
He knew how long they had remained.
He understood the danger of sending them away hungry.
And His compassion moved toward their need.
But then the disciples asked a question that sounds painfully familiar.
“Whence should we have so much bread in the wilderness, as to fill so great a multitude?” — Matthew 15:33, KJV
In other words:
Where are we supposed to find enough?
Enough bread.
Enough resources.
Enough provision.
Enough to meet a need this overwhelming.
Have you ever asked God the same question?
Lord, where will the money come from?
Where will I find the strength?
How can this family be restored?
How can this addiction be overcome?
How can I rebuild after everything I have destroyed?
How can You possibly use someone with my history?
The disciples were looking at the size of the crowd and the limitations of their surroundings.
And their question was understandable.
The need was real.
The wilderness was real.
Their resources were genuinely insufficient.
But standing in front of them was Someone greater than the wilderness.
Jesus asked:
“How many loaves have ye?” — Matthew 15:34, KJV
Their answer?
“Seven, and a few little fishes.”
Seven loaves.
A few small fish.
Thousands of hungry people.
From a human perspective, the numbers were almost insulting.
The resources were so small compared with the need that even attempting to feed the crowd could seem absurd.
Yet Jesus did not panic.
He did not complain about what they lacked.
He did not dismiss the crowd because the disciples had insufficient supplies.
He instructed the people to sit down.
Then Matthew records:
“And he took the seven loaves and the fishes, and gave thanks, and brake them, and gave to his disciples, and the disciples to the multitude.” — Matthew 15:36, KJV
Notice the order.
Jesus took what was available.
He gave thanks.
He broke the bread.
He gave it to the disciples.
And the disciples distributed it to the people.
The miracle was Christ's work.
The disciples were servants through whom the provision reached the crowd.
That distinction is important.
We do not create God's power by offering Him something.
We do not force miracles through religious formulas.
And this passage is not a guarantee that giving away your last money or possessions will cause God to multiply them materially.
The point is far greater.
Jesus Christ was sufficient for a need that human resources could not meet.
And the people ate.
Not a symbolic mouthful.
Not a tiny portion to make the bread stretch.
Matthew 15:37 says:
“And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the broken meat that was left seven baskets full.” — KJV
There it is.
The sentence that changes the way we look at this entire miracle.
They all ate.
They were filled.
And seven baskets remained.
The Greek text reads:
καὶ ἔφαγον πάντες καὶ ἐχορτάσθησαν, καὶ τὸ περισσεῦον τῶν κλασμάτων ἦραν, ἑπτὰ σπυρίδας πλήρεις.
Transliteration: kai ephagon pantes kai echortasthēsan, kai to perisseuon tōn klasmatōn ēran, hepta spyridas plēreis.
A close English rendering is:
“And they all ate and were satisfied, and they took up what remained of the broken pieces, seven full baskets.”
Pay attention to the word ἐχορτάσθησαν (echortasthēsan).
It means they were satisfied or filled.
The crowd was not merely given enough food to delay hunger for another hour.
They ate until they were satisfied.
And the word περισσεῦον (perisseuon) refers to what remained or was left over.
The leftovers were not the result of a failed miracle.
They were evidence that the provision had exceeded what the crowd consumed.
But here is where we must read carefully.
Why exactly seven baskets?
Many Christians have heard that seven always represents divine perfection or completeness.
There is a biblical basis for associating seven with completion in certain contexts, especially in the creation account, where God completed His work and rested on the seventh day.
But that does not mean every appearance of the number seven automatically carries the same symbolic message.
Matthew never explicitly says the seven baskets represent seven blessings, seven spiritual gifts, seven nations, or seven categories of divine provision.
We should not pretend that he does.
The text gives us the number.
It does not provide a direct symbolic explanation for that number.
So we need to distinguish what Scripture clearly teaches from what may be a thoughtful theological reflection.
And once we do that, the miracle becomes more beautiful, not less.
Because the first answer to why seven baskets remained is wonderfully simple.
Seven baskets remained because Jesus had provided more food than the crowd needed to eat.
The leftovers demonstrated the abundance of His provision.
The exact number also became a memorable detail that Jesus Himself later used when reminding His disciples of what they had witnessed.
And there is another detail hidden in the original Greek that makes this account even more interesting.
The word Matthew uses for baskets is σπυρίδας (spyridas), the plural of σπυρίς (spyris).
This is not the same Greek word used for the baskets in the feeding of the five thousand.
In Matthew 14:20, the twelve baskets are described using κόφινοι (kophinoi).
In Matthew 15:37, the seven baskets are spyrides.
These words identify different types of baskets.
The spyris could be a relatively large basket; the same Greek word is used in Acts 9:25 for the basket in which Paul was lowered through an opening in the Damascus wall.
That does not prove every basket in Matthew 15 was identical in size to the one used for Paul.
But it does show that the word could describe something substantially larger than a small lunch container.
Seven full baskets of remaining food.
After approximately four thousand men had eaten, besides women and children.
Imagine the scene.
People who had arrived hungry were now satisfied.
Families who had wondered where food could be found were no longer searching.
The disciples were gathering the remaining pieces.
One basket filled.
Then another.
Then another.
Until seven baskets stood before them.
And perhaps the disciples remembered something.
Because this was not the first time Jesus had done this.
Earlier, in Matthew 14, Jesus had fed five thousand men, besides women and children, with five loaves and two fish.
Twelve baskets remained.
Now, in Matthew 15, He fed four thousand men, besides women and children, beginning with seven loaves and a few fish.
Seven baskets remained.
These were two distinct miracles.
Not two confused versions of the same event.
And we know this because Jesus Himself later referred to both.
In Matthew 16:9–10, He asked His disciples:

“Do ye not yet understand, neither remember the five loaves of the five thousand, and how many baskets ye took up? Neither the seven loaves of the four thousand, and how many baskets ye took up?” — KJV
Jesus deliberately reminded them of both miracles and their different basket counts.
Five loaves.
Five thousand.
Twelve baskets.
Seven loaves.
Four thousand.
Seven baskets.
The details mattered enough for Jesus to bring them back into the conversation.
But why?
Read the surrounding passage.
The disciples were worried because they had forgotten to bring bread.
And Jesus challenged their failure to understand.
They had witnessed His provision twice, yet their thoughts were still trapped inside the limitations of what they could carry.
They remembered that they had no bread.
But they were failing to reckon with the One who was standing beside them.
That is the piercing lesson.
They had seen Jesus provide abundantly, but they were still afraid of scarcity.
And before we judge them, perhaps we should examine ourselves.
How many times has God carried us through a season we thought would destroy us?
How many prayers have we seen answered?
How many doors have opened when we thought everything was finished?
How many times have we survived a grief, a failure, a loss, or a crisis that once seemed impossible to endure?
Yet when the next difficulty comes, fear begins speaking as though we have never known the faithfulness of God.
We forget.
Not always because we have rejected Jesus.
Sometimes because our pain is loud.
Our circumstances are immediate.
And yesterday's testimony feels distant when today's need is staring us in the face.
The disciples needed to remember.
So do we.
But remembering does not mean pretending that every prayer receives the answer we want.
The same Lord who fed the crowd also calls His followers to take up their cross.
Faith does not exempt us from suffering.
God's provision is not always a visible surplus.
Sometimes His grace sustains us through circumstances He has not yet removed.
Sometimes He provides through the generosity of others.
Sometimes through ordinary work, wise decisions, unexpected help, or strength to endure another day.
And sometimes we do not understand His ways at all.
The miracle of the seven baskets should never be used to shame someone who is struggling financially, grieving deeply, or waiting for an answer to prayer.
It is not a formula for wealth.
It is a revelation of Jesus.
The center of the story is not a number.
The center is the Savior whose compassion moved Him to feed the hungry.
And that brings us to something even greater than the bread.
Because the greatest hunger of the human soul cannot be satisfied by anything we can hold in our hands.
You can have a full refrigerator and an empty heart.
You can have a successful career and a conscience burdened by guilt.
You can have thousands of followers and still feel completely alone.
You can have money, recognition, relationships, and comfort, yet lie awake at night wondering why nothing seems to quiet the ache inside you.
There is a hunger that success cannot feed.
A shame that applause cannot erase.
A guilt that time alone cannot forgive.
A separation from God that no amount of religious activity can repair.
And this is where the miracle points us toward the larger Gospel story.
In John 6:35, Jesus declared:
“I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.” — KJV
This statement comes from John's account of Jesus' ministry in connection with the feeding of the five thousand, not the feeding of the four thousand.
We should preserve that distinction.
Yet together, these passages reveal a consistent truth about Christ.
He does not merely give bread.
He is the Bread of Life.
The physical bread in Matthew 15 satisfied real physical hunger.
But Jesus Himself offers something no earthly food can provide.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness of sins.
Eternal life.
A new heart.
A new beginning.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are not simply hungry.
We are ashamed.
We remember what we did.
The words we cannot take back.
The relationship we destroyed.
The promises we broke.
The secret habit we keep returning to.
The years we wasted.
The person we pretended to be.
We have learned how to look respectable while carrying memories that still make us feel unworthy of love.
And somewhere deep inside, a terrible question keeps returning.
Could Jesus still want someone like me?
Look at the people who came to Him in Matthew 15.
They did not arrive with impressive résumés.
They arrived with needs.
They brought weakness.
Suffering.
Desperation.
And Jesus received the crowds and ministered to them.
But the Gospel goes even further than compassion for human weakness.
It confronts our sin and reveals God's saving mercy.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we made our histories respectable.
Not after we became worthy through our own goodness.
Christ died for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did something infinitely greater than multiplying bread.
He bore sin.
He gave His life.
He accomplished the saving work that no human being could accomplish.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The risen Christ calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what we have done.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is refusing to defend the darkness while asking Jesus to transform the heart.
And forgiveness is not God pretending our sins never mattered.
It is mercy made possible through the sacrifice of Christ.
That is why grace is so astonishing.
It does not tell us our sin was harmless.
It tells us that Jesus is a greater Savior than our sin.
And perhaps that is the message someone desperately needs today.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may carry consequences you still have to face.
It may require confession, restitution, accountability, and difficult changes.
But your past does not possess the authority to declare that the grace of Jesus Christ is insufficient.
The cross has already answered that question.
And the resurrection has announced that death does not have the final word.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Not because the consequences vanished.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
Consider Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
He had insisted that he would remain faithful.
Then fear exposed him.
The rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice denying the Lord you claimed to love.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
So was Christ's restoring grace.
Consider the apostle Paul.
He had persecuted the church.
His history was not a minor mistake.
Yet the risen Jesus confronted him, and the persecutor became a servant of the Gospel he once opposed.
Paul never needed to pretend his past had been innocent.
He testified to the mercy of Christ.
And if Jesus could restore Peter and save Paul, who are we to declare that our failures are beyond His reach?
This does not mean every person will receive the same calling or experience the same circumstances.
It means no sinner should assume that the saving power of Christ is too small for their need.
The miracle of the seven baskets is not a direct allegory about the forgiveness of seven kinds of sin.
Matthew never says that.
But the compassion and sufficiency revealed in Jesus' ministry are entirely consistent with the Gospel of the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And that is the connection worth holding onto.
The crowd could not manufacture enough bread.
Sinners cannot manufacture their own righteousness.
The crowd depended on Christ's provision.
We depend on Christ's saving grace.
The crowd was physically satisfied by the food He gave.
Those who come to Christ in repentance and faith receive the salvation that only He can give.
And now we return to the question.
Why were seven baskets left over?
Because Jesus provided abundantly, and Matthew faithfully recorded what remained.
Because those baskets became part of a miracle the disciples were supposed to remember.
Because the visible evidence of Christ's provision challenged their fear and unbelief.
And because this account continues to direct our attention toward the compassionate authority of the Lord Jesus.
We may reflect on the biblical associations of the number seven with completeness.
We may consider the possible significance of the wider Gentile context.
But we must not claim certainty where Scripture does not provide it.
The miracle does not need invented symbolism to become powerful.
The truth is already enough.
Jesus saw the hungry.
Jesus had compassion.
Jesus gave thanks.
Jesus provided.
The people were satisfied.
And seven baskets remained.
What a Savior.
Not a distant religious figure who merely delivers instructions.
Not a cold judge who delights in human suffering.
But the holy Son of God, full of truth and compassion, who came into a broken world to accomplish the redemption we could never earn.
And here is the question that may be more important than why seven baskets remained.
What are you doing with the Jesus who provided them?
Because it is possible to admire the miracle and refuse the Savior.
It is possible to be fascinated by Greek words, biblical numbers, and historical details while remaining unwilling to surrender your life to Christ.
You can understand the meaning of spyris and still refuse to repent.
You can explain the difference between the feeding of the five thousand and the four thousand while continuing to hide the very sin Jesus is calling you to confess.
Knowledge matters.
Sound doctrine matters.
Faithful interpretation matters.
But biblical understanding should lead us toward worship, obedience, repentance, and deeper trust in Christ.
Not merely toward winning arguments.
Not merely toward collecting interesting facts.
And certainly not toward treating Jesus as a means of acquiring whatever we want.
He is Lord.
He is Savior.
He is worthy of our lives.
So perhaps today is the day to stop hiding behind the appearance of being fine.
Perhaps today is the day to confess the bitterness you have been nursing.
To abandon the secret compromise you keep excusing.
To return to prayer after months of spiritual silence.
To seek forgiveness from someone you have wounded.
To ask for help with a struggle you can no longer overcome by pretending it does not exist.
Or perhaps you are not running from God at all.
Perhaps you are simply tired.
Tired of carrying grief.
Tired of being strong.
Tired of wondering whether your prayers are heard.
Then hear the words of Jesus in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — KJV
Come to Him.
Not to a promise of effortless living.
Not to a guarantee that tomorrow will be painless.
Come to the Savior who is gentle and lowly in heart.
The Savior who died and rose again.
The Savior who is worthy of your trust even when you cannot understand the road ahead.
And if this message has uncovered something in your heart, do not rush past that moment.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to publish your deepest wounds for strangers to see.
But you can make a simple declaration of faith, surrender, or hope.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus met you in a season of weakness, consider sharing it.
Someone reading the comments may be fighting a battle they have never told anyone about.
Your testimony might remind them to turn toward Christ rather than surrender to despair.
There is another way to respond to this message.
Think of one person who needs to remember the compassion of Jesus.
A friend who has stopped attending church.
A brother who has quietly lost hope.
A daughter who feels ashamed of her past.
A believer who has been faithful for years but is now spiritually exhausted.
A person who does not yet know Christ.
Send them this article.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone more righteous.
Not because God measures devotion by social media activity.
But because the Gospel is worth communicating, and one thoughtful act of sharing can place biblical encouragement before someone who might never have searched for it.
You never know who may read quietly without reacting.
Who may return to the Scriptures.
Who may finally ask someone for prayer.
Who may begin asking serious questions about Jesus.
There may come a day when the circumstances in front of you seem much larger than the faith you feel inside.
On that day, return to Matthew 15.
Remember the crowd.
Remember the compassion.
Remember the bread.
Remember the seven baskets.
Most importantly, remember Jesus.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who has questions.
Invite the one who has become spiritually complacent.
Invite the seeker who is not yet sure what to believe.
We want Gospel Warrior to remain a place where people are directed back to Scripture, challenged to examine their hearts, and encouraged to know Jesus Christ more deeply.
It is voluntary financial support for the ongoing work of producing and sharing Christian teaching, encouragement, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered messages.
It helps make continued ministry possible and supports the effort to reach more people with biblical truth.
Scripture encourages believers to give generously, willingly, and according to their ability.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Not from guilt.
Not from fear.
And not because a monthly payment can replace the biblical responsibilities of stewardship, generosity, or support for your local church.

If Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you to return to Jesus, and you are financially able to contribute, we invite you to prayerfully consider becoming a monthly supporter.
For others, it may mean sharing the message, praying for the ministry, or encouraging someone to read the Bible.
Every form of sincere support has value.
These resources and products are intended to encourage faith, support discipleship, and help keep biblical truth present in everyday life.
Our desire is that believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ can continue learning, studying, praying, and strengthening their understanding of God's Word.
The free resources remain a meaningful part of that mission.
But please remember something.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ, received by faith, not a reward for financial support.
What we are inviting you into is a shared mission: helping biblical truth reach more people while growing together in Scripture, prayer, and discipleship.
Because when the final day comes, the question will not be how many Christian products you purchased or how many ministries you supported.
What matters eternally is whether you belong to Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Repent and believe.
Receive the forgiveness that He alone provides.
Follow Him.
And let His Word transform the way you live.
Now return with me, one final time, to that hillside.
The crowds have eaten.
The children are no longer hungry.
The families are preparing to leave.
The disciples are gathering what remains.
Seven baskets.
Full.
The people had arrived with needs they could not meet.
And Jesus had not turned them away.
But the greatest wonder is not the amount of bread left behind.
It is the identity of the One who stood among them.
The same Jesus who had compassion on that hungry multitude would go to the cross for sinners.
The hands that broke the bread would be pierced.
The One who satisfied the crowd would willingly endure suffering to accomplish our redemption.
And the grave would not hold Him.
He rose.
He lives.
And He still calls people to turn from sin and follow Him.
So if you have spent years believing your story is too damaged, too shameful, or too complicated for God to redeem, look again at the cross.
Your sin is serious.
Your need is real.
But Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
And if you have already trusted Him, do not allow the fear of tomorrow to erase your memory of His faithfulness.
Keep walking with Him.
Keep opening His Word.
Keep praying.
Keep repenting when you fall.
Keep trusting when the road is difficult.
Keep remembering that your hope rests not in your ability to hold everything together, but in the finished work and continuing faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
The seven baskets were eventually emptied.
The bread was eaten.
The crowd went home.
But the testimony of what Jesus did has endured for generations.
And now it has reached you.
Not so that you would become obsessed with a mysterious number.
But so that you would behold the Savior.
Above everything else, give your heart and your life to Jesus.
Because the most beautiful thing about the seven baskets is not what remained after the people were filled—it is the Savior who was standing there when they had nothing.
